{{short description|Mathematical sequence}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''k''-regular sequence}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical computer science]], a '''''k''-regular sequence''' is a [[sequence]] satisfying linear recurrence equations that reflect the [[Positional notation|base-''k'' representations]] of the integers. The class of ''k''-regular sequences generalizes the class of [[automatic sequence|''k''-automatic sequences]] to alphabets of infinite size.

==Definition==
There exist several characterizations of ''k''-regular sequences, all of which are equivalent. Some common characterizations are as follows. For each, we take ''R''′ to be a [[commutative]] [[Noetherian ring]] and we take ''R'' to be a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] containing ''R''′.

===''k''-kernel===
Let ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2. The ''k-kernel'' of the sequence <math>s(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> is the set of subsequences
:<math>K_{k}(s) = \{s(k^e n + r)_{n \geq 0} : e \geq 0 \text{ and } 0 \leq r \leq k^e - 1\}.</math>
The sequence <math>s(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> is (''R''′, ''k'')-regular (often shortened to just "''k''-regular") if the <math>R'</math>-module generated by ''K''<sub>''k''</sub>(''s'') is a [[Finitely generated module|finitely-generated]] ''R''′-[[module (mathematics)|module]].<ref name=AS21>Allouche and Shallit (1992), Definition 2.1.</ref>

In the special case when <math>R' = R = \mathbb{Q}</math>, the sequence <math>s(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> is <math>k</math>-regular if <math>K_k(s)</math> is contained in a finite-dimensional vector space over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.

===Linear combinations===
A sequence ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-regular if there exists an integer ''E'' such that, for all ''e''<sub>''j''</sub> > ''E'' and 0 ≤ ''r''<sub>''j''</sub> ≤ ''k''<sup>''e''<sub>''j''</sub></sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1, every subsequence of ''s'' of the form ''s''(''k''<sup>''e''<sub>''j''</sub></sup>''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''r''<sub>''j''</sub>) is expressible as an ''R''′-[[linear combination]] <math>\sum_{i} c_{ij} s(k^{f_{ij}}n + b_{ij})</math>, where ''c''<sub>''ij''</sub> is an integer, ''f''<sub>''ij''</sub> ≤ ''E'', and 0 ≤ ''b''<sub>''ij''</sub> ≤ ''k''<sup>''f''<sub>''ij''</sub></sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1.<ref name=AS22>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 2.2.</ref>

Alternatively, a sequence ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-regular if there exist an integer ''r'' and subsequences ''s''<sub>1</sub>(''n''), ..., ''s''<sub>''r''</sub>(''n'') such that, for all 1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''r'' and 0 ≤ ''a'' ≤ ''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1, every sequence ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>(''kn''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a'') in the ''k''-kernel ''K''<sub>''k''</sub>(''s'') is an ''R''′-linear combination of the subsequences ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>(''n'').<ref name=AS22 />

===Formal series===
Let ''x''<sub>0</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sub> be a set of ''k'' non-commuting variables and let τ be a map sending some natural number ''n'' to the string ''x''<sub>''a''<sub>0</sub></sub> ... ''x''<sub>''a''<sub>''e''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sub></sub>, where the base-''k'' representation of ''x'' is the string ''a''<sub>''e''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sub>...''a''<sub>0</sub>. Then a sequence ''s''(''n'') is ''k''-regular if and only if the [[Formal power series|formal series]] <math>\sum_{n \geq 0} s(n) \tau (n)</math> is <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-[[Rational series|rational]].<ref name=AS43>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 4.3.</ref>

===Automata-theoretic===
The formal series definition of a ''k''-regular sequence leads to an automaton characterization similar to [[Marcel-Paul Schützenberger|Schützenberger]]'s matrix machine.<ref name=AS44>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 4.4.</ref><ref>{{citation | last = Schützenberger | first = M.-P. | title = On the definition of a family of automata | journal = Information and Control | volume = 4 | issue = 2–3 | year = 1961 | pages = 245–270 | doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(61)80020-X | doi-access = free }}.</ref>

==History==
The notion of ''k''-regular sequences was first investigated in a pair of papers by Allouche and Shallit.<ref name=AS>Allouche & Shallit (1992, 2003).</ref> Prior to this, Berstel and Reutenauer studied the theory of [[rational series]], which is closely related to ''k''-regular sequences.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Berstel | first1 = Jean | last2 = Reutenauer | first2 = Christophe | title = Rational Series and Their Languages | volume = 12 | series = EATCS Monographs on Theoretical Computer Science | year = 1988 | isbn = 978-3-642-73237-9 | publisher = [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]] }}</ref>

==Examples==

===Ruler sequence===
Let <math>s(n) = \nu_2(n+1)</math> be the [[p-adic valuation | <math>2</math>-adic valuation]] of <math>n+1</math>. The ruler sequence <math>s(n)_{n \geq 0} = 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, \dots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id=A007814}}) is <math>2</math>-regular, and the <math>2</math>-kernel
:<math>\{s(2^e n + r)_{n \geq 0} : e \geq 0 \text{ and } 0 \leq r \leq 2^e - 1\}</math>
is contained in the two-dimensional vector space generated by <math>s(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> and the constant sequence <math>1, 1, 1, \dots</math>. These basis elements lead to the recurrence relations
:<math>
\begin{align}
s(2 n) &= 0, \\
s(4 n + 1) &= s(2 n + 1) - s(n), \\
s(4 n + 3) &= 2 s(2 n + 1) - s(n),
\end{align}
</math>
which, along with the initial conditions <math>s(0) = 0</math> and <math>s(1) = 1</math>, uniquely determine the sequence.<ref name=ASe8>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Example 8.</ref>

===Thue–Morse sequence===
The [[Thue–Morse sequence]] ''t''(''n'') ({{OEIS2C|id=A010060}}) is the [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] of the morphism 0 → 01, 1 → 10. It is known that the Thue–Morse sequence is 2-automatic. Thus, it is also 2-regular, and its 2-kernel
:<math>\{t(2^e n + r)_{n \geq 0} : e \geq 0 \text{ and } 0 \leq r \leq 2^e - 1\}</math>
consists of the subsequences <math>t(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> and <math>t(2 n + 1)_{n \geq 0}</math>.

===Cantor numbers===
The sequence of [[Cantor set|Cantor numbers]] ''c''(''n'') ({{OEIS2C|id=A005823}}) consists of numbers whose [[Ternary numeral system|ternary]] expansions contain no 1s. It is straightforward to show that 
:<math>
\begin{align}
c(2n) &= 3c(n), \\
c(2n+1) &= 3c(n) + 2,
\end{align}
</math>
and therefore the sequence of Cantor numbers is 2-regular. Similarly the [[Stanley sequence]]
:0, 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12, 13, 27, 28, 30, 31, 36, 37, 39, 40, ... {{OEIS|A005836}}
of numbers whose ternary expansions contain no 2s is also 2-regular.<ref name=ASe3>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Examples 3 and 26.</ref>

===Sorting numbers===
A somewhat interesting application of the notion of ''k''-regularity to the broader study of algorithms is found in the analysis of the [[merge sort]] algorithm. Given a list of ''n'' values, the number of comparisons made by the merge sort algorithm are the [[sorting number]]s, governed by the recurrence relation
:<math>
\begin{align}
T(1) &= 0, \\
T(n) &= T(\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor) + T(\lceil n / 2 \rceil)  + n - 1, \ n \geq 2.
\end{align}
</math>
As a result, the sequence defined by the recurrence relation for merge sort, ''T''(''n''), constitutes a 2-regular sequence.<ref name=ASe28>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Example 28.</ref>

===Other sequences===
If <math>f(x)</math> is an [[integer-valued polynomial]], then <math>f(n)_{n \geq 0}</math> is ''k''-regular for every <math>k \geq 2</math>.

The [[Gould's sequence|Glaisher–Gould]] sequence is 2-regular. The Stern–Brocot sequence is 2-regular.

Allouche and Shallit give a number of additional examples of ''k''-regular sequences in their papers.<ref name=AS />

==Properties==
''k''-regular sequences exhibit a number of interesting properties.
*Every [[automatic sequence|''k''-automatic sequence]] is ''k''-regular.<ref>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 2.3.</ref>
*Every [[k-synchronized sequence|''k''-synchronized sequence]] is ''k''-regular.
*A ''k''-regular sequence takes on finitely many values if and only if it is ''k''-automatic.<ref name=AS441>Allouche & Shallit (2003) p. 441.</ref> This is an immediate consequence of the class of ''k''-regular sequences being a generalization of the class of ''k''-automatic sequences.
*The class of ''k''-regular sequences is closed under termwise addition, termwise multiplication, and [[convolution]]. The class of ''k''-regular sequences is also closed under scaling each term of the sequence by an integer λ.<ref name=AS441 /><ref>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 2.5.</ref><ref>Allouche & Shallit (1992), Theorem 3.1.</ref><ref name=AS445>Allouche & Shallit (2003) p. 445.</ref> In particular, the set of ''k''-regular [[power series]] forms a ring.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 446.</ref>
*If <math>s(n)_{n \ge 0}</math> is ''k''-regular, then for all integers <math>m \ge 1</math>, <math>(s(n) \bmod{m})_{n \ge 0}</math> is ''k''-automatic. However, the converse does not hold.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 441.</ref> 
*For multiplicatively independent ''k'',&nbsp;''l''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2, if a sequence is both ''k''-regular and ''l''-regular, then the sequence satisfies a linear recurrence.<ref>{{cite journal | first=J. | last=Bell | title=A generalization of Cobham's theorem for regular sequences| journal=Séminaire Lotharingien de Combinatoire | volume=54A | year=2006 }}</ref> This is a generalization of a result due to Cobham regarding sequences that are both ''k''-automatic and ''l''-automatic.<ref>{{cite journal | first=A. | last=Cobham | title=On the base-dependence of sets of numbers recognizable by finite automata | journal=Math. Systems Theory | volume=3 | issue=2 | year=1969 | pages=186–192 | doi=10.1007/BF01746527 | s2cid=19792434 }}</ref>
*The ''n''th term of a ''k''-regular sequence of integers grows at most polynomially in ''n''.<ref>Allouche & Shallit (1992) Theorem 2.10.</ref>
*If <math>F</math> is a field and <math>x \in F</math>, then the sequence of powers <math>(x^n)_{n \ge 0}</math> is ''k''-regular if and only if <math>x = 0</math> or <math>x</math> is a [[root of unity]].<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 444.</ref>

==Proving and disproving ''k''-regularity==
Given a candidate sequence <math>s = s(n)_{n \ge 0}</math> that is not known to be ''k''-regular, ''k''-regularity can typically be proved directly from the definition by calculating elements of the kernel of <math>s</math> and proving that all elements of the form <math>(s(k^r n + e))_{n \ge 0}</math> with <math>r</math> sufficiently large and <math>0 \le e < 2^r</math> can be written as linear combinations of kernel elements with smaller exponents in the place of <math>r</math>. This is usually computationally straightforward.

On the other hand, disproving ''k''-regularity of the candidate sequence <math>s</math> usually requires one to produce a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-linearly independent subset in the kernel of <math>s</math>, which is typically trickier. Here is one example of such a proof.

Let <math>e_0(n)</math> denote the number of <math>0</math>'s in the binary expansion of <math>n</math>. Let <math>e_1(n)</math> denote the number of <math>1</math>'s in the binary expansion of <math>n</math>. The sequence <math>f(n) := e_0(n)-e_1(n)</math> can be shown to be 2-regular. The sequence <math>g = g(n) := |f(n)|</math> is, however, not 2-regular, by the following argument. Suppose <math>(g(n))_{n \ge 0}</math> is 2-regular. We claim that the elements <math>g(2^k n)</math> for <math>n \ge 1</math> and <math>k \ge 0</math> of the 2-kernel of <math>g</math> are linearly independent over <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>. The function <math>n \mapsto e_0(n)-e_1(n)</math> is surjective onto the integers, so let <math>x_m</math> be the least integer such that <math>e_0(x_m)-e_1(x_m) = m</math>. By 2-regularity of <math>(g(n))_{n \ge 0}</math>, there exist <math>b \ge 0</math> and constants <math>c_i</math> such that for each <math>n \ge 0</math>,
:<math>\sum_{0 \le i \le b} c_i g(2^i n) = 0.</math>

Let <math>a</math> be the least value for which <math>c_a \ne 0</math>. Then for every <math>n \ge 0</math>,
:<math>g(2^a n) = \sum_{a+1 \le i \le b} -(c_i/c_a) g(2^i n).</math>

Evaluating this expression at <math>n = x_m</math>, where <math>m = 0,-1,1,2,-2</math> and so on in succession, we obtain, on the left-hand side
:<math>g(2^a x_m) = |e_0(x_m)-e_1(x_m)+a| = |m+a|,</math>

and on the right-hand side,
:<math>\sum_{a+1 \le i \le b} -(c_i/c_a)|m+i|.</math>

It follows that for every integer <math>m</math>,
:<math>|m+a| = \sum_{a+1 \le i \le b} -(c_i/c_a) |m+i|.</math>

But for <math>m \ge -a-1</math>, the right-hand side of the equation is monotone because it is of the form <math>Am+B</math> for some constants <math>A,B</math>, whereas the left-hand side is not, as can be checked by successively plugging in <math>m = -a-1</math>, <math>m = -a</math>, and <math>m = -a+1</math>. Therefore, <math>(g(n))_{n \ge 0}</math> is not 2-regular.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (1993) p. 168–169.</ref>
